paper.title: Work-related violence and depressive disorder among 955,573 employees followed for 6.99 million person-years. The Danish Work Life Course Cohort study
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The article states that it is 'Based on a pre-published study protocol' and that 'The design and analyses were pre-defined in a pre-published protocol (Madsen et al., 2018b)'; …

variables_mentioned: F92.0, 308.02 (used only to exclude pre-entry cases)

registers.role: outcome (depressive disorder diagnoses, incl. outpatient from 1995)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Health services register
registers.role: control (number of health services used in the year before workforce entry, mainly primary health care)

registers.name_in_paper: Danish registers on personal income and transfer payments (Baadsgaard and Quitzau, 2011)
registers.role: controls (income, employment status, main source of income used to define workforce entry)
linkage and controls (gender, age, ethnicity, cohabitation, children, migration, death)

registers.name_in_paper: job exposure matrix (JEM) constructed using survey data from the Danish Work Environment Cohort Study
registers.role: treatment (gender- and age-specific probability of work-related violence by occupation)
variables_mentioned: occupation coded in the Danish version of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-88)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Work Life Course Cohort (DaWCo)
registers.role: sample frame (open inception cohort of first-time entrants to the Danish workforce)

linkages: Individuals linked to parental psychiatric and somatic diagnoses and to parental education and labour market status; linkage to parental data available from 1980 onwards and only for individuals with parents residing in Denmark (11.3% missing maternal data, 12.6% missing paternal data)
Individuals linked to an occupational job exposure matrix through their occupational code (Danish version of ISCO-88), by gender and age
Individuals linked to psychiatric in- and outpatient admissions in the Psychiatric Central Research Register and the National Patient Register

sample.universe: All individuals who first entered the Danish workforce during 1995-2009 and were 15 to 30 years old at entry (Danish Work Life Course Cohort, DaWCo)
selection_rules: Workforce entry defined as the first year with employment as the main source of income (n=979,257)
Excluded individuals with missing data on gender and ethnicity (n=5,176)
Excluded individuals who died (n=71), emigrated (n=13,087) or received disability pension (n=361) in their year of entry, leaving 960,562
Excluded individuals with diagnosed depressive disorder before or in the year of workforce entry (n=4,989)
Final cohort 955,573 individuals followed for 6,991,811 person-years (mean follow-up 7.3 years)
Follow-up from workforce entry until first depressive disorder diagnosis, death, emigration, receipt of disability pension, or 31 December 2010, whichever came first
Follow-up limited to 2010 because exposures could not be updated after 2009 due to changes in the occupational classification

construction_notes: Work-related violence measured by a job exposure matrix giving the average gender- and age-specific probability of work-related violence by occupation (Danish ISCO-88); JEM built on Danish Work Environment Cohort Study survey data; AUC 0.89 against self-report in that study, 0.84 (men) and 0.86 (women) in an independent sample
Each person-year assigned an annual exposure probability, set to 0 in years of non-employment
Cumulated exposure = sum of the annual probabilities over the work life
Both past-year and cumulated exposure log2-transformed (a small constant added first to avoid log(0)) and entered as continuous variables, so hazard ratios are per doubling of exposure probability
Categorical past-year exposure: low (0 to <1% probability), medium (1 to 2%), high (>2%), built from the quartiles of exposure probability with the first two quartiles collapsed
A further categorical measure of the proportion of previous annual measures with high risk of violence: 0 to 5%, 6% to 25%, 26% to 75%, 76% or more
Pearson correlation between past-year and cumulated work-related violence risk: 0.74

Depressive disorder: main diagnosis F32/F33 (ICD-10, 1994-2010) or 296.0, 296.2, 298.0, 300.4 (ICD-8, 1969-1993); F92.0 and 308.02 used additionally to exclude pre-entry cases; ICD-9 never used in Denmark

Age, cohabitation, number of children, education, income, employment status, years of non-employment and years of work experience included as annual time-varying variables; remaining covariates time-invariant

Childhood socioeconomic position measured by maternal and paternal educational level and labour market status when the cohort member was 15 years old; individuals with missing parental data retained and adjusted for with missing-data categories
One-year time lag: exposure in year t related to events in year t+1; calendar time used as the time axis
16,148 incident cases during 6,991,811 person-years, i.e. 23 cases per 10,000 person-years

claims.statement: A doubling of the past-year occupational probability of work-related violence is associated with a 1% higher hazard of a first hospital diagnosis of depressive disorder (Model 1).

treatment.label: Past year work-related violence, per doubling of exposure probability

register_source.value: Job exposure matrix built from Danish Work Environment Cohort Study survey data, applied to occupation coded in the Danish version of ISCO-88; the paper names no register variable code

definition.value: Annual gender- and age-specific probability of work-related violence in the individual's occupation, read off a job exposure matrix (JEM) and assigned to each person-year, with probability 0 in years of non-employment; log2-transformed (after adding a small constant to avoid log(0)) and entered as a continuous variable, so the hazard ratio is per doubling of the exposure probability. Entered in the same model as cumulated exposure (mutually adjusted).

timing.value: Measured in year t (the past year), related to events in year t+1

outcome.label: First diagnosis of depressive disorder (incident hospital-treated depressive disorder)

register_source.value: The Psychiatric Central Research Register (1969-1994) and The National Patient Register (1995-2010); the paper names no register variable codes

definition.value: Time to first hospital diagnosis of depressive disorder, defined as a main diagnosis of F32 or F33 (ICD-10, years 1994 to 2010) or 296.0, 296.2, 298.0, 300.4 (ICD-8, years 1969 to 1993), taken from psychiatric inpatient admissions (from 1969) and outpatient admissions (from 1995); individuals diagnosed with depressive disorder (incl. F92.0 / 308.02) before or in the year of workforce entry were excluded, so the measure is incident. 16,148 cases occurred during 6,991,811 person-years (23 cases per 10,000 person-years).

timing.value: Followed from workforce entry until first depressive disorder diagnosis, death, emigration, receipt of disability pension, or end of follow-up 31 December 2010; events in year t+1 are related to exposure in year t

units.value: hazard ratio per doubling of the past-year probability of work-related violence

magnitude.interpretation: As an example of interpretation, this estimate shows that individuals with 4% probability of work-related violence had a hazard ratio of 1.01 compared to individuals with a 2% probability of work-related violence (p. 138).

estimand.target_population: Employees in Denmark followed from first workforce entry at ages 15-30 in 1995-2009
estimand.time_horizon: One-year lag: exposure during year t related to events during year t+1, over a follow-up from workforce entry to 31 December 2010 (mean follow-up 7.3 years)
estimand.formal_query: h(t | do(log2 past-year WRV probability = x+1), X) / h(t | do(log2 past-year WRV probability = x), X)

population.ages: 15 to 30 years old at cohort entry
population.selection: Cohort entry required first employment as the main source of income at ages 15-30 during 1995-2009 (n=979,257); individuals with missing gender or ethnicity (n=5,176) and those who died (n=71), emigrated (n=13,087) or received disability pension (n=361) in their entry year were excluded, as were individuals with diagnosed depressive disorder before or in the year of workforce entry (n=4,989), leaving 955,573 individuals.
population.description: 955,573 individuals who first entered the Danish workforce in 1995-2009 aged 15-30 and were free of diagnosed depressive disorder before or in their entry year (the Danish Work Life Course Cohort), followed for 6,991,811 person-years (mean follow-up 7.3 years)

identification.source_of_variation: Between-occupation differences in the job-exposure-matrix probability of work-related violence, as employees move through jobs after entering the workforce. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity: the design is an observational inception-cohort comparison adjusted for pre-workforce-entry risk factors.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates (gender, age, cohabitation, ethnicity, number of children, employment status (employed vs. non-employed, with studying and self-employment as dummies)), the probability of work-related violence in a person-year is unrelated to the person's underlying risk of depressive disorder -- i.e. the adjustment set blocks the selection of individuals vulnerable to depression into occupations with high risk of violence.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states it adjusted for risk factors pre-existing workforce entry in order to account for this selection, and reports that results were similar when parental data were omitted and when individuals with any prior psychiatric diagnosis were excluded.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exposure precedes outcome: a one-year time lag relates exposure in year t to events in year t+1, so depressive disorder does not cause the measured exposure (no reverse causation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The design itself (one-year lag) plus exclusion of anyone diagnosed with depressive disorder before or in the year of workforce entry; the authors concede the lag is a limitation if effects are acute and triggering.

implies_edges.from: first hospital-diagnosed depressive disorder
implies_edges.to: past year probability of work-related violence (JEM, log2)

key_assumptions.assumption: Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio for work-related violence is constant over the calendar-time axis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual inspection of log-log hazard plots (no test statistic reported).

key_assumptions.assumption: No confounding by vulnerability factors the registers do not carry -- in particular life events and genetics.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue a life-events explanation would have been attenuated by adjustment for childhood socioeconomic position and was not; they nevertheless list the lack of life-event and genetic data as a limitation.

implies_edges.from: unmeasured vulnerability (life events, genetics)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exposure misclassification by the job exposure matrix is non-differential with respect to depressive disorder (the JEM measures occupation-level, not individual-level, violence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A quantitative bias analysis (Lash, Fox & Fink 2009) assuming sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.80, and JEM validation against self-report (AUC 0.89).

key_assumptions.assumption: Censoring at death, emigration, receipt of disability pension or 31 December 2010 is independent of the depressive-disorder hazard given the covariates (non-informative censoring).

implies_edges.from: censoring at death, emigration or disability pension

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the cohort on first workforce entry at age 15-30 in 1995-2009 and on being free of diagnosed depressive disorder before or in the entry year does not itself bias the exposure-outcome association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that following people from workforce entry diminishes healthy-worker selection and that the register design avoids selective participation and drop-out.

implies_edges.from: cohort entry: first workforce entry at age 15-30 in 1995-2009, free of depressive disorder at entry

treatment.label: Cumulated work-related violence, per doubling

register_source.value: Job exposure matrix built from Danish Work Environment Cohort Study survey data, applied to occupation coded in the Danish version of ISCO-88; the paper names no register variable code

definition.value: Exposure cumulated over the work life, constructed by summing the annual JEM probabilities of work-related violence up to year t; log2-transformed (after adding a small constant) and entered as a continuous variable, so the hazard ratio is per doubling of cumulated exposure. Entered in the same model as past-year exposure (mutually adjusted).

timing.value: Cumulated from workforce entry through year t, related to events in year t+1

outcome.label: First diagnosis of depressive disorder (incident hospital-treated depressive disorder)

register_source.value: The Psychiatric Central Research Register (1969-1994) and The National Patient Register (1995-2010); the paper names no register variable codes

definition.value: Time to first hospital diagnosis of depressive disorder, defined as a main diagnosis of F32 or F33 (ICD-10, years 1994 to 2010) or 296.0, 296.2, 298.0, 300.4 (ICD-8, years 1969 to 1993), taken from psychiatric inpatient admissions (from 1969) and outpatient admissions (from 1995); individuals diagnosed with depressive disorder (incl. F92.0 / 308.02) before or in the year of workforce entry were excluded, so the measure is incident. 16,148 cases occurred during 6,991,811 person-years (23 cases per 10,000 person-years).

timing.value: Followed from workforce entry until first depressive disorder diagnosis, death, emigration, receipt of disability pension, or end of follow-up 31 December 2010; events in year t+1 are related to exposure in year t

units.value: hazard ratio per doubling of cumulated probability of work-related violence

estimand.target_population: Individuals of non-danish ethnicity among employees in Denmark followed from first workforce entry at ages 15-30 in 1995-2009
estimand.time_horizon: One-year lag: exposure during year t related to events during year t+1, over a follow-up from workforce entry to 31 December 2010 (mean follow-up 7.3 years)
estimand.formal_query: h(t | do(log2 cumulated WRV = x+1), X, stratum=Non-Danish ethnicity) / h(t | do(log2 cumulated WRV = x), X, stratum=Non-Danish ethnicity)

population.ages: 15 to 30 years old at cohort entry
population.selection: Cohort entry required first employment as the main source of income at ages 15-30 during 1995-2009 (n=979,257); individuals with missing gender or ethnicity (n=5,176) and those who died (n=71), emigrated (n=13,087) or received disability pension (n=361) in their entry year were excluded, as were individuals with diagnosed depressive disorder before or in the year of workforce entry (n=4,989), leaving 955,573 individuals.
population.description: 955,573 individuals who first entered the Danish workforce in 1995-2009 aged 15-30 and were free of diagnosed depressive disorder before or in their entry year (the Danish Work Life Course Cohort), followed for 6,991,811 person-years (mean follow-up 7.3 years), restricted to individuals of non-Danish ethnicity

identification.source_of_variation: Between-occupation differences in the job-exposure-matrix probability of work-related violence, as employees move through jobs after entering the workforce. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity: the design is an observational inception-cohort comparison adjusted for pre-workforce-entry risk factors.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates (age, cohabitation, number of children, employment status, years of non-employment, years of work experience), the probability of work-related violence in a person-year is unrelated to the person's underlying risk of depressive disorder -- i.e. the adjustment set blocks the selection of individuals vulnerable to depression into occupations with high risk of violence.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states it adjusted for risk factors pre-existing workforce entry in order to account for this selection, and reports that results were similar when parental data were omitted and when individuals with any prior psychiatric diagnosis were excluded.

ambiguities: The covariate set for the industry x gender analysis is not printed in the article; the adjustment recorded here is the one stated for the other stratified analyses (Table 4 note). Detailed results are in Supplementary Table S5, which is not part of the article PDF.

The 'Cases per 10.000 PY' value printed on the row (15) is the rate for the whole gender x industry stratum, not for the low-exposure reference group; it is recorded as the baseline mean for want of a printed reference-group rate.

The HR and 95% CI printed for Manufacturing are identical in the MEN and the WOMEN panel (0.72, 0.52-1.01) while the P-values differ (0.052 vs 0.005); the figure may duplicate a row. Transcribed as printed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates (age, cohabitation, number of children, employment status, years of non-employment, years of work experience), the probability of work-related violence in a person-year is unrelated to the person's underlying risk of depressive disorder -- i.e. the adjustment set blocks the selection of individuals vulnerable to depression into occupations with high risk of violence.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states it adjusted for risk factors pre-existing workforce entry in order to account for this selection, and reports that results were similar when parental data were omitted and when individuals with any prior psychiatric diagnosis were excluded.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exposure precedes outcome: a one-year time lag relates exposure in year t to events in year t+1, so depressive disorder does not cause the measured exposure (no reverse causation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The design itself (one-year lag) plus exclusion of anyone diagnosed with depressive disorder before or in the year of workforce entry; the authors concede the lag is a limitation if effects are acute and triggering.

key_assumptions.assumption: Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio for work-related violence is constant over the calendar-time axis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual inspection of log-log hazard plots (no test statistic reported).

key_assumptions.assumption: No confounding by vulnerability factors the registers do not carry -- in particular life events and genetics.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue a life-events explanation would have been attenuated by adjustment for childhood socioeconomic position and was not; they nevertheless list the lack of life-event and genetic data as a limitation.

implies_edges.from: unmeasured vulnerability (life events, genetics)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exposure misclassification by the job exposure matrix is non-differential with respect to depressive disorder (the JEM measures occupation-level, not individual-level, violence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A quantitative bias analysis (Lash, Fox & Fink 2009) assuming sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.80, and JEM validation against self-report (AUC 0.89).

key_assumptions.assumption: Censoring at death, emigration, receipt of disability pension or 31 December 2010 is independent of the depressive-disorder hazard given the covariates (non-informative censoring).

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the cohort on first workforce entry at age 15-30 in 1995-2009 and on being free of diagnosed depressive disorder before or in the entry year does not itself bias the exposure-outcome association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that following people from workforce entry diminishes healthy-worker selection and that the register design avoids selective participation and drop-out.

evidence.how: The reference-group outcome rate for the same cohort and the same high/medium vs. low contrast is printed in Table 3: 23 depression cases per 10 000 person-years in the low-exposure category. The supplementary models differ from Table 3 only in which covariates are adjusted for, so the low-exposure incidence rate is unchanged.
